questions.question: Which pair of laboratories forms inertial reference frames relative to each other?
options: Two laboratories moving at constant relative velocity
A laboratory and a rocket firing its engine
Two laboratories rotating around each other
A laboratory and a rocket firing its boosters
questions.explanation: Inertial frames move with constant relative velocity and have no acceleration between them. Acceleration or rotation makes the listed frame non-inertial for this definition.
questions.sourceEvidence: Special relativity describes measurements made in inertial reference frames, which move at constant velocity relative to one another.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Classifying an accelerating or rotating frame as inertial

questions.question: What does Einstein's first postulate say about inertial frames?
options: One hidden frame has simpler laws
The laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame
Light defines an absolute stationary laboratory
questions.explanation: Every inertial observer expresses physical laws in the same form. The postulate rejects a privileged inertial frame rather than limiting equivalence to mechanics.
questions.sourceEvidence: Einstein’s first postulate states that the laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming one inertial frame is physically privileged

questions.question: Can an experiment performed entirely inside a sealed laboratory moving uniformly reveal its absolute speed?
options: Yes, by detecting an absolute speed with internal light signals
Yes, by measuring its own clock rate
No, absolute rest cannot be identified internally
Only when the laboratory moves east
questions.explanation: Uniform motion has no internally detectable absolute rest standard. Local measurements can reveal relative motion or acceleration but not a preferred inertial state.
questions.sourceEvidence: No internal experiment performed in a uniformly moving laboratory can identify an absolute state of rest.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Believing uniform absolute motion can be detected without an external reference

questions.question: How do two inertial observers moving relative to each other measure the speed of the same vacuum light pulse?
options: The faster observer obtains a speed above c
They obtain speeds separated by their relative velocity
Only the source observer obtains c
questions.explanation: The second postulate requires every inertial observer to measure vacuum light at c. Ordinary Galilean addition does not apply to the measured speed of light.
questions.sourceEvidence: The second postulate states that light in vacuum has the same speed c for every inertial observer, independent of the motion of the source or observer.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Adding source or observer velocity directly to the speed of light

questions.question: Why must space and time transform together between inertial frames?
options: To preserve the same measured light speed
To make all objects share one rest frame
questions.explanation: Lorentz transformations mix space and time so every inertial observer still measures light at c. They do not remove relative motion or create universal simultaneity.
questions.sourceEvidence: Space and time must therefore transform together through Lorentz transformations so that every inertial observer obtains the same light speed.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using a space-only Galilean transformation while demanding invariant light speed

questions.question: Two separated flashes are simultaneous in one inertial frame. What must another moving frame conclude?
options: Their order must reverse in every case
questions.explanation: Simultaneity of separated events depends on the observer's inertial frame. There is no universal time slice that all moving observers must share.
questions.sourceEvidence: Events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating simultaneity of separated events as absolute

questions.question: Which interpretation of time dilation and length contraction is physically correct?
options: They are mechanical damage caused by speed
They are frame-dependent measurements rooted in simultaneity
They disappear after correcting clock calibration
questions.explanation: The effects follow from how inertial frames relate space and time measurements. They persist after optical delays and instrument errors are corrected.
questions.sourceEvidence: Relativity of simultaneity is the foundation from which time dilation and length contraction follow; they are not optical illusions or mechanical distortions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Dismissing relativistic measurements as visual or mechanical artifacts

questions.question: What geometric quantity do inertial observers agree on despite assigning different space and time components?
questions.explanation: Observers divide spacetime differently but calculate the same invariant interval between events. They generally disagree about the separate spatial and temporal components.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hermann Minkowski later expressed the theory geometrically as spacetime, in which different observers divide the same invariant interval into different spatial and temporal components.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Expecting observers to agree on space and time separately instead of on the interval

questions.question: Which clock measures the proper time between two events?
options: A single clock present at both events
A clock moving past both events
The fastest clock in the experiment
questions.explanation: Proper time is recorded by one clock that is physically present at both events. A clock that occupies different locations from the events measures a coordinate-time interval instead.
questions.sourceEvidence: Proper time Δτ is the interval measured by a single clock present at both events.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Choosing proper time from convenience rather than one-clock event coincidence

questions.question: A moving clock records 3 seconds of proper time while γ = 2. What coordinate time does the observer measure?
questions.explanation: Time dilation gives Δt = 2 times 3 seconds, which is 6 seconds. Dividing by the Lorentz factor would apply the relation in the wrong direction.
questions.sourceEvidence: An observer who sees that clock move measures a longer coordinate-time interval Δt = γΔτ.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Dividing rather than multiplying proper time by the Lorentz factor

questions.question: Between the same departure and reunion events, which clock accumulates less proper time?
options: The coordinate grid rather than a clock
Every clock accumulates identical proper time
The clock following the moving spacetime path
questions.explanation: The moving clock follows a path that accumulates less proper time between the reunion events. Proper time depends on the spacetime path rather than brightness or a universal clock rate.
questions.sourceEvidence: Because γ is at least one, moving clocks accumulate less proper time between the same pair of reunion events.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming elapsed proper time is path-independent

questions.question: When is the reciprocal description of time dilation directly symmetric?
options: While both observers remain in equivalent inertial situations
questions.explanation: Each observer may regard the other inertial clock as moving while their situations remain equivalent. Acceleration or unequal spacetime paths breaks the simple reciprocal setup at reunion.
questions.sourceEvidence: The effect is reciprocal only while the observers remain in equivalent inertial situations.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Extending inertial reciprocity unchanged through acceleration and reunion

questions.question: Why does a moving light clock tick more slowly in an observer's coordinates?
options: Its light follows a longer diagonal path at the same speed c
Its pulse loses energy on each reflection
questions.explanation: The moving geometry lengthens the pulse path while both observers retain the same light speed. The explanation does not require slower light or a damaged clock.
questions.sourceEvidence: To an observer who sees the clock move sideways, the pulse follows a longer diagonal path.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Explaining time dilation by changing the speed of light

questions.question: When does the Lorentz factor differ appreciably from one?
options: Only when v is a significant fraction of c
Only when an object is at rest
questions.explanation: Relativistic time dilation becomes large only as speed approaches a substantial fraction of c. Ordinary speeds leave the Lorentz factor extremely close to one.
questions.sourceEvidence: The Lorentz factor becomes appreciable only when v is a significant fraction of c.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Expecting large time dilation at ordinary speeds

questions.question: Why do unstable particles produced in accelerators survive far longer in the laboratory than their rest-frame lifetimes predict?
options: Laboratory observers measure the moving particle's internal decay clock as time-dilated
questions.explanation: Laboratory observers measure the fast-moving particle's internal clock as running slower by the Lorentz factor, extending the observed lifetime. The explanation requires neither superluminal travel nor an external field halting decay.
questions.sourceEvidence: Time dilation has direct experimental evidence. Unstable particles produced in high-energy accelerators survive far longer in the laboratory than their rest-frame lifetimes would allow, because laboratory observers measure the moving particle's internal clock as time-dilated.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Explaining extended particle lifetimes in the laboratory without relativistic time dilation

questions.question: Why must high-precision timing systems that track fast-moving particles include relativistic clock corrections?
options: The speed of light varies inside accelerators
Particle detectors cannot send radio signals
Atomic clocks stop near particle beams
Moving clocks accumulate measurable relativistic offsets
questions.explanation: Time dilation shifts the readings of moving clocks by measurable amounts. The corrections address clock rates rather than failed signal transmission or variable vacuum light speed.
questions.sourceEvidence: Atomic clocks transported on aircraft have accumulated measurable relativistic offsets consistent with special-relativistic predictions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating relativistic clock offsets as too small to matter in precision experiments

questions.question: In which frame is an object's proper length measured?
options: Any frame in which it moves
The frame with the shortest ruler
questions.explanation: Proper length is defined in the frame where the object is at rest. A moving observer measures a contracted length rather than the proper length.
questions.sourceEvidence: Proper length L0 is measured in the rest frame of an object by recording its endpoints.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling a moving-frame length the proper length

questions.question: A rod has proper length 12 metres and moves with γ = 3 parallel to its length. What length is measured?
questions.explanation: Length contraction gives 12 metres divided by 3, which is 4 metres. Multiplying by the Lorentz factor reverses the contraction relation.
questions.sourceEvidence: An observer who sees the object moving parallel to its length measures L = L0/γ.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Multiplying proper length by the Lorentz factor

questions.question: Which dimensions of a moving rectangular box contract?
options: Only the dimension parallel to motion
questions.explanation: Lorentz contraction affects the longitudinal dimension parallel to relative motion. Transverse dimensions are unchanged rather than shrinking isotropically.
questions.sourceEvidence: Contraction occurs only along the direction of relative motion; transverse dimensions are unchanged.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying length contraction to transverse dimensions

questions.question: What physically happens to a fast rod because of length contraction?
options: Different frames make different valid length measurements
questions.explanation: Length contraction describes frame-dependent coordinate measurements of the same intact object. It is not mechanical compression, heating, or mass loss.
questions.sourceEvidence: It is a difference between valid frame-dependent measurements, not damage to the object.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Interpreting length contraction as physical damage

questions.question: What measurement procedure is required to find the length of a moving object?
options: Record both endpoints simultaneously in the observer's frame
Record the front now and the back much later
Photograph it without correcting light travel time
Use the object's wristwatch at one endpoint
questions.explanation: A spatial length joins endpoint positions taken at the same observer time. Using endpoint events at different times mixes motion into the measured separation.
questions.sourceEvidence: Measuring a moving length requires recording both endpoint positions simultaneously in the observer’s frame.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Measuring moving endpoints at different observer times

questions.question: Why does another inertial frame disagree with the endpoint pair used for a moving-length measurement?
options: Light has different speeds in the frames
questions.explanation: A pair of separated events simultaneous in one frame is generally not simultaneous in another. The disagreement follows from spacetime coordinates rather than ruler construction or changing light speed.
questions.sourceEvidence: Because simultaneity is frame-dependent, another frame does not regard those endpoint measurements as simultaneous.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Ignoring relativity of simultaneity in length measurement

questions.question: Why may a photograph of a relativistic object not show the simple calculated contracted shape?
options: Photographs include unequal light-travel times from different points
questions.explanation: A photograph collects light emitted from different positions at different times, adding optical timing effects. The coordinate length formula assumes simultaneous endpoint positions rather than raw arrival times at a camera.
questions.sourceEvidence: Photographs also include light-travel-time effects and do not directly display the simple contracted shape calculated from simultaneous coordinates.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Equating a photographic appearance with a simultaneous-coordinate length

questions.question: How does a fast particle explain reaching a distant detector within its short proper lifetime?
options: The detector moves faster than light
The separation has zero length in every frame
The particle's proper lifetime increases in its own frame
The distance to the detector is length-contracted in the particle's frame
questions.explanation: In the particle's rest frame the laboratory distance to the detector is longitudinally contracted, so the detector arrives within the particle's ordinary proper lifetime. The particle's own proper lifetime remains unchanged and no object exceeds c.
questions.sourceEvidence: In the laboratory frame, a fast particle's internal clock is time-dilated; in the particle's rest frame, the distance to the target detector is length-contracted. Both frames predict the same collision events because Lorentz transformations preserve their causal relationships.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying time dilation to the particle clock in the particle's own rest frame

questions.question: What energy does a particle of invariant mass m possess in its rest frame?
options: E0 = hf for every massive particle
questions.explanation: Invariant mass corresponds to rest energy through E0 = mc². A massive particle retains rest energy even when its momentum is zero.
questions.sourceEvidence: A particle of invariant mass m has rest energy E0 = mc².
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming a stationary massive particle has zero total energy

questions.question: What happens to a particle's invariant mass as its speed increases?
questions.explanation: Modern relativistic treatment keeps the particle's invariant mass fixed across frames. Motion increases total energy and momentum rather than the invariant mass.
questions.sourceEvidence: The relation means mass is one form of energy, not that an object’s invariant mass simply increases with speed.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using the obsolete idea that invariant mass grows with speed

questions.question: Which expression gives the total energy of a moving massive particle?
questions.explanation: A moving massive particle has total energy γmc². The expression pc alone is the massless limit, while the other formulas omit the relativistic factor.
questions.sourceEvidence: Modern treatments keep m invariant and describe a moving particle with total energy E = γmc² and momentum p = γmv.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing rest energy, classical kinetic energy, and relativistic total energy

questions.question: A particle moves with γ = 3. What is its kinetic energy in units of mc²?
questions.explanation: Relativistic kinetic energy is γ minus one times mc², giving 2 mc². Using γmc² would give total energy and include the rest energy.
questions.sourceEvidence: Kinetic energy is the difference K = (γ − 1)mc².
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reporting total energy as kinetic energy

questions.question: Which relation connects a particle's total energy, momentum, and invariant mass?
questions.explanation: The energy-momentum invariant combines the momentum term and rest-energy term in quadrature. Classical kinetic energy is only a low-speed approximation and cannot replace the invariant relation.
questions.sourceEvidence: Energy and momentum satisfy E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using a classical energy formula at relativistic speed

questions.question: What energy-momentum relation applies to a photon?
options: E = 0 because its invariant mass is zero
questions.explanation: Setting invariant mass to zero leaves E = pc for a photon. Zero invariant mass does not mean zero energy or momentum.
questions.sourceEvidence: For a massless particle, this reduces to E = pc; photons have zero invariant mass but carry energy and momentum.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Concluding that a massless photon has no energy or momentum

questions.question: Why can a bound composite system have a mass different from the sum of its isolated component masses?
options: Internal kinetic and binding energies contribute to the system invariant mass
Only electric charge determines composite mass
questions.explanation: The system's internal energy contributes to its invariant mass as a whole. Adding isolated rest masses alone can omit binding and internal kinetic energy.
questions.sourceEvidence: The invariant mass of a composite system can include internal kinetic and binding energies, so it need not equal the sum of isolated component masses.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Adding component rest masses while ignoring internal energy

questions.question: In nuclear fission, where can a decrease in final rest mass appear?
options: As an absolute loss of energy
questions.explanation: A reduction in system rest mass is released as other forms of energy such as motion or radiation. Mass-energy equivalence preserves total energy rather than destroying it.
questions.sourceEvidence: A decrease in system mass appears as kinetic energy or radiation; an increase requires supplied energy.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating mass difference in a reaction as destroyed energy

questions.question: What should be identified before selecting a relativity formula?
options: The two events and the reference frame
The observer with the newest clock
questions.explanation: Relativistic quantities are defined by particular events and frames, so both must be labelled first. Choosing a formula from speed alone often reverses proper and coordinate quantities.
questions.sourceEvidence: Always identify the two events and the frame before choosing a formula.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying a relativity formula before defining its events and frame

questions.question: Which description correctly pairs the proper quantities with their frames?
options: Proper time is always the larger interval, and proper length uses any moving frame
Proper time uses one clock at both events, and proper length uses the object rest frame
Proper time uses two synchronized clocks, and proper length is the shortest measurement
Both proper quantities belong to an absolute rest frame
questions.explanation: One co-located clock defines proper time while the object rest frame defines proper length. Proper does not mean largest, smallest, or measured in a preferred universal frame.
questions.sourceEvidence: Proper time is measured by one clock present at both events; proper length is measured in the object’s rest frame.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Defining proper quantities by magnitude rather than measurement conditions

questions.question: How are a moving clock and a moving length measured relative to their proper quantities?
options: The clock interval is dilated and the longitudinal length is contracted
The clock interval is contracted and the length is dilated
questions.explanation: Coordinate time exceeds proper time while moving longitudinal length is less than proper length. Applying the Lorentz factor in the same direction to both quantities ignores their definitions.
questions.sourceEvidence: A moving clock is time-dilated, while a moving length is contracted along motion.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying the Lorentz factor in the wrong direction

questions.question: After correcting all light-travel delays, what can still differ between inertial frames?
options: The occurrence of a single local event
questions.explanation: Relativity of simultaneity is a coordinate effect that remains after signal delays are removed. It is not an illusion caused by photons taking time to reach an observer.
questions.sourceEvidence: Simultaneity itself is frame-dependent after such delays are corrected.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reducing relativity of simultaneity to signal delay

questions.question: Why does reciprocal inertial time dilation not create a contradiction when travellers reunite?
options: Reunion generally involves acceleration or unequal spacetime paths
questions.explanation: A reunion comparison includes the full spacetime paths, which need not remain inertially equivalent. No preferred stationary frame or faulty clock is required to resolve the elapsed-time difference.
questions.sourceEvidence: Apparent reciprocity in time dilation does not create a contradiction when observers reunite, because reunion generally requires acceleration or unequal spacetime paths.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying reciprocal inertial symmetry to unequal reunion paths

questions.question: Which mass concept should be used in modern relativity?
options: Relativistic mass that grows with speed
Coordinate mass that changes by direction
questions.explanation: Invariant mass provides a frame-independent property while energy and momentum transform. Calling increased total energy increased mass obscures the modern invariant definition.
questions.sourceEvidence: Use invariant mass rather than “relativistic mass.”
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating speed-dependent relativistic mass as the particle invariant

questions.question: Why can no massive object be accelerated to c?
options: The Lorentz factor and required energy diverge
questions.explanation: As speed approaches c, γ grows without bound and so does the required energy. The barrier is energetic and geometric rather than caused by charge or a reverse force from light.
questions.sourceEvidence: Massive objects cannot reach c because γ and required energy diverge as v approaches c.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming finite energy can accelerate a massive object to light speed

questions.question: Which statement about a photon is valid?
options: It has a rest frame moving at c
It travels below c when observed from a fast rocket
It accumulates ordinary proper time like a massive clock
It travels at c in vacuum but has no valid rest frame
questions.explanation: Every inertial observer measures a vacuum photon at c, and no Lorentz frame can move alongside it. Assigning a photon rest frame violates the structure of inertial Lorentz transformations.
questions.sourceEvidence: Photons always travel at c in vacuum and have zero proper time along a lightlike path, but there is no valid photon rest frame.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Inventing a photon rest frame
